title: Azure portal, Cloud Shell, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell and Azure Arc
learningObjective: Describe the Azure portal, Azure Cloud Shell, Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell, and the purpose of Azure Arc.
foundation: Azure portal: a website (portal.azure.com) to create, manage and monitor everything in Azure with clicks, plus customisable dashboards.
Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell: command-line tools to do the same things with commands, which you can save as scripts and repeat. CLI commands start with az; PowerShell uses cmdlets like Get-AzVM.
Azure Cloud Shell: a command line in your browser, already signed in, with both tools installed. Nothing to install on your PC.
Azure Arc: brings servers, Kubernetes clusters and databases running outside Azure (on-premises, other clouds) into Azure, so you manage them with the same tools.
engineer: Portal: build, manage and monitor from simple web apps to complex deployments; create custom dashboards; set accessibility options; designed for resiliency and continuous availability, present in every Azure datacenter, updated continuously with no downtime.

Cloud Shell: choose Bash or PowerShell; authenticated with your Azure credentials; includes Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell and common tools (git, kubectl, terraform, editors); optional file share for persistent $HOME storage. Open from the portal toolbar or shell.azure.com.

Azure CLI: cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux); syntax az <group> <command> --params, for example az vm create. Azure PowerShell: the Az module of cmdlets (Verb-Noun), for example New-AzVM; runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with PowerShell 7. Both are functionally equivalent for most tasks; pick the one your team knows. Both support interactive use and scripts.

Azure Arc: manage servers (Windows/Linux), Kubernetes clusters, Azure data services (SQL Managed Instance, PostgreSQL) and SQL Server outside Azure. Once connected they appear as Azure resources (projected into Azure Resource Manager): apply Azure Policy, RBAC, tags, monitoring (Azure Monitor), security (Defender for Cloud) and updates consistently.
Use Arc when: you have a hybrid or multicloud estate, need one governance model across environments, or want Azure services to run where your data lives.

example.title: A hybrid operations team
body: Operators use the portal dashboards to watch production, run quick fixes from Cloud Shell on locked-down laptops, and schedule nightly Azure CLI scripts in a pipeline.
120 on-premises Linux servers and an AWS Kubernetes cluster are connected with Azure Arc, so the same tagging policy and Defender for Cloud plans apply everywhere.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription (a free account works)
permissions: Reader to explore; Contributor to create resources
portal: Portal toolbar > Cloud Shell icon (Bash or PowerShell).
Azure Arc > Machines > Add/Create > Add a single server (generates an onboarding script).
configuration.cli:
az login
az group list -o table
az connectedmachine list -o table
configuration.powershell:
Connect-AzAccount
Get-AzResourceGroup | Format-Table ResourceGroupName, Location
Get-AzConnectedMachine

steps: Management tools tab: answer every task.
Azure CLI, PowerShell, Cloud Shell tab: identify every command.
failureScenarios: Installing tools on a locked-down PC instead of using Cloud Shell
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.fix: Install it or use Cloud Shell.

troubleshooting.symptom: On-premises servers don't appear in Azure Policy compliance.
troubleshooting.fix: Onboard them with the Arc Connected Machine agent.

comparisons.difference: Same capabilities, different syntax: Bash-style commands vs PowerShell cmdlets and objects.
Arc projects resources into Azure management; VPN only connects networks.

misconceptions.myth: Cloud Shell runs on your computer.
misconceptions.reality: It runs in Azure, in a container, accessed through the browser.

misconceptions.myth: Azure PowerShell only runs on Windows.

misconceptions.reality: They stay where they are; Arc manages them.

architectureDecisions: Use the portal to explore, scripts to repeat.
Standardise on CLI or PowerShell per team.
Use Arc for consistent hybrid governance.
